blocks.text: And the hyena the panther (supply δυσμενῆ κρινεῖ [dysmenē krinei], considers hostile, which is to be repeated from the preceding [col. 1086]) and the thieving destroyer scorpion the stellio, but numbness seizes it. For in Aelian's words, νάρκη γοῦν τὸν σκορπίον καταλαμβάνει [narkē goun ton skorpion katalambanei], the word νάρκη [narkē] is not the torpedo [electric ray] fish, but the torpor [numbness] which seizes the scorpion when it sees the stellio. If, with some, you correct it to ναρκοῖ δὲ τοῦτον [narkoi de touton], but it (the scorpion) numbs it (the stellio), Phile would have said something utterly false, namely that the stellio is numbed by the scorpion, whereas on the contrary the stellio numbs the scorpion. Indeed Democritus, Pliny, Galen, Aëtius, Diophanes and others prescribe a stellio cut open, steeped in oil and left to putrefy, as an effective remedy against the stings of scorpions. Nor is it of slight weight that even today in the vulgar tongue of the Greeks the stellio is called σαμιαμίνθη [samiaminthē], a name plainly distorted from the Hebrew שממית semamith. The Glossae: Ἀσκαλαβώτης· τὸ σαμιαμίνθη [Askalabōtēs; to samiaminthē]. By Gesner it is written θαμιάμιθος [thamiamithos] and ψαμαμύθη [psamamythē]; by Bellonius SAMIAMITOS, who wrongly takes it for the Chalcidian lizard. See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 1161.

There are some who write שׁממית schemamith with Shin, as if it came from שמם schamam, that is, to stupefy. This itself fits well the nature of the stellio, which stupefies the scorpion by its mere sight, as we have shown. But in Kimchi and in the purest copies of the Bible it is written שׂממית semamith with Sin Semol, just as סממית with Samech in the Talmudic writings and in the Samaritan paraphrase. Thus it is to be derived from סמם, not from שמם, that is, from poison, not from stupor. So, to understand the true reason for the name, one must know that two species of stellio are reported: one with a harmless bite, the other with a venomous one. The writers, however, do not agree in which places they are born. The Philosopher ^{c)} assigns the venomous ones to Italy and Sicily, the harmless ones to Greece. [II, 514] On the other hand Theophrastus, in Pliny, book 8, chapter 31, states that stellios, deadly in their bite in Greece, are harmless in Sicily. In Thrace too the stellio has a pernicious bite, as is found in Nicander. And Bustamantinus of Complutum asserts that stellios are so pernicious that, mixed by chance with food, they have laid waste entire populations. Hence Aëtius, Paulus and Avicenna prescribe so many remedies against the bite of the stellio. And Columella, book 10, chapter 7, wants the openings of beehives to be very narrow, lest the venomous stellio ravage the combs through the wider spaces of the entrance. He added the epithet venomous διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs], because another kind is harmless. The name stellio suits the venomous one better, if Verrius, in Varro and Festus, truly asserts that the stellio is so called because it drips venom. To the same was given the name סממית semamith, because סם sam among the Hebrews and Syrians is φάρμακον [pharmakon], or poison; and in Arabic سم [samm] samma is the verb to infect with poison. Therefore סממית semamith is properly σαῦρα φαρμακὶς [saura pharmakis], or φαρμακῖτις [pharmakitis]. I see that this very name is used by the Greeks in a sense little different. Nicander in the Alexipharmaca, line 537:
Φαρμακίδος σαύρης πολυμήδεος, ἣν σαλαμάνδρην Κλείουσιν. — — — — — — — [Pharmakidos saurēs polymēdeos, hēn salamandrēn Kleiousin.]

You see that there the σαῦρα φαρμακίς [saura pharmakis] is the salamander, a kind of lizard so similar to the stellio that some take it for a species of stellio. Accordingly the Scholiast there: Ἡ σαλαμάνδρα· εἶδος ἀσκαλαβώτου [Hē salamandra; eidos askalabōtou]. Yet in Aëtius, Tetrab. 4, Serm. 4, ch. 52, the salamander, the stellio and the venomous lizard, in Greek σαῦρα φαρμακῖτις [saura pharmakitis], are different little animals, but very similar to one another. The salamander, he says, is an animal similar to the stellio, rougher, and more scaly than the venomous lizard. Perhaps by the name stellio he means only the harmless one, and by the name pharmacitis lizard, or venomous lizard, distinct from the salamander, the stellio with a harmful bite. Thus the pharmacitis lizard will be the same as the סממית semamith.
